vignette:
He is seventy-six now, a slight South Eastern Asian man with careful hands and a back that stiffens by the end of a warehouse shift. He has never married. For years he has worked in receiving, standing beside loading docks, checking manifests, counting boxes, and waving younger men toward the right pallets. He likes work that can be measured and finished. He says little at first about why he prefers the dull thud of cartons and the predictability of inventory sheets. Only after several meetings does the shape of his life begin to emerge, and it begins in the war.

As a young man, he is living in a town where ordinary life narrows slowly, then all at once. At first there are rumors, then shortages, then soldiers on roads he used to travel without thinking. He remembers his mother still trying to cook rice as if routine might hold the walls in place. He remembers people lowering their voices, glancing toward the door before speaking. Then the shelling starts close enough to rattle dishes and send everyone to the ground. One afternoon he is outside when an explosion tears through the market street ahead of him. He does not tell the story dramatically. He says there is a flash, a force in his chest, and then confusion—dust so thick he cannot understand what he is seeing. A bicycle wheel spins without a bicycle. Someone is screaming for a child. He smells burning metal and something else he does not name.

After that, the world changes its rules. He moves from one relative’s house to another, sleeps in clothes that are ready for running, and learns to read danger in small shifts of sound. When aircraft pass overhead, his whole body locks before his mind catches up. He sees wounded civilians carried on doors and blankets. He helps when he can, lifting, fetching water, digging. He also sees people he knows disappear from one week to the next. At night he lies awake waiting for the next blast, trying not to breathe too loudly. He tells himself that if he stays alert enough, he can keep his family alive. Even now, he speaks of that period with a kind of shame, as though surviving required compromises he still cannot fully forgive.

Eventually he leaves. The journey out is fragmented in his memory: crowded transport, long waiting, fear of being turned back, the strain of trying not to show fear to others. In the new country, people tell him he is safe, but safety does not arrive with him. He finds factory and warehouse jobs because they do not require many words and because labor gives him a way to move without thinking. He works hard, keeps to himself, sends money when he can, and builds a life that from the outside looks stable. Inside, he remains braced.

For decades he sleeps lightly. He wakes before dawn, sometimes from dreams in which he is back in the market street, unable to find his mother in the smoke. On those mornings he sits at the edge of the bed, already sweating, listening for sounds that do not belong in his apartment. He keeps a small flashlight nearby even though the electricity is reliable. Loud bangs still go through him like electricity. At work, if a pallet drops unexpectedly or a truck backfires in the loading bay, he flinches hard enough that the younger workers look over. He laughs it off and says he is just old, but afterward his heart races for a long time and he has to pretend to study a clipboard until his hands stop trembling.

He avoids certain things without always admitting that he is avoiding them. He does not watch war footage on television. He takes longer routes to avoid construction sites where heavy machinery slams metal against concrete. He rarely attends community events on holidays because fireworks undo him. He says crowds are tiring, but what he means is that too many bodies, too much noise, and no clear exit make him feel trapped. He prefers his apartment arranged exactly the same way, shoes by the door, documents in a folder, canned food lined up in the cupboard. He knows this makes him seem rigid. To him it feels like preparedness.

There is loneliness in the life he has built. He has friends at work in a practical sense—men who nod to him, share tea, ask about his knees—but he does not let people get close enough to ask what happened before he came here. He says there is no use burdening others. Yet the memories come uninvited anyway: the smell of dust after rain, the whine of an engine overhead, a woman in the grocery store calling sharply for her son. In those moments he is no longer an old warehouse worker with a scanner in his hand. He is a young man in a street blown open, scanning for the living among the broken things.

What troubles him now is not only the memory itself but the endurance of it. He thought time would have finished this work by now. Instead, he notices how quickly his body still chooses alarm, how often his mind returns to the dead, how hard it is to rest even in a quiet room. He has survived long enough to grow old, yet part of him remains fixed in that earlier world, listening for danger, unwilling to believe that the day can simply pass without catastrophe.
